meta.title: The C Form: Where Fragments Come From
meta.summary: The C form's grip is the open C chord you already play, but barre it anywhere else and the root sits three frets past the barre — which is exactly why fragments exist.

spans.text: Here's the honest complication: for C major, the C form is the open C chord, and the open C chord is easy. It's easy because the nut is doing the barring for free. Move this form anywhere else on the neck and the problem this lesson is about shows up immediately.

You already know its two roots from chapter 1 — string 5, fret 3, and string 2, fret 1. This lesson fills in the notes around them, and it is the first window where you can actually count the gap between what the diagram holds and what a hand does.

spans.text: Now here's precisely why the full barre fails once you move off the nut. Barre at fret
on string 1. The highest fretted note is three frets past the barre, and it's the root — the one note you can't afford to drop. Barre the C form at fret 5 and you get
, and a stretch almost nobody's hand wants to hold.

Compare that to the A form, coming next: its full barre never asks for more than two frets past itself. The C form asks for three, and the note stranded out there is the one note the chord can't do without. That's not a technique problem to practice your way past — it's the shape of the neck saying this form wants to be played differently once it leaves the nut.
So real players don't hold it whole. They take fragments straight out of the same window: strings 4-3-2 give you

— two compact triads, no four-fret stretch required. And on the barred version, the standard dodge is simpler still: skip string 1 and let the other four ring. These aren't workarounds for a shape that's secretly broken. They're the normal way this form gets played.
Strings 3-2-1 alone give you a full triad, root included, with nothing to stretch for. That's the C form in the position most players actually reach for it.
